2.text: shape of a strong wooden stick (Fig. 21, a¹). In Kamchatka the brake is

3.text: slightly curved, while that of other countries is straight. It has a bunch of

4.text: jingling rings on one end, and a sharp iron spike on the other. A short

5.text: strap is tied to the jingling end. The driver holds the brake with his right

6.text: hand, and when required checks the motion of the sledge by thrusting the
6.note: mz/ocr keyed a comma after 'the' ("checks the, motion"); at 2x zoom this is a small low stray ink speck, not a comma or period shape - no punctuation belongs there. Also a similar speck sits below 'checks'. Keyed as plain text with no punctuation.

7.text: brake into the snow close in front of the first right stanchion. The brake is

8.text: used to prevent the sledge from overturning or to raise it when overturned,

9.text: to slacken the pace when the dogs go too fast, and, in connection with the

10.text: word of command, to stop the team.

11.text: When a dog is disobedient on the way, the driver jingles the rings of

12.text: the brake, or strikes the brake against the standing bow. Sometimes he

13.text: throws it over the head of the animal, being careful, however, to hit it with

14.text: the jingling end, because the spike would kill it outright. After the brake

15.text: is thrown, the driver has to pick it up very quickly; otherwise the team might

16.text: go ahead, leaving the driver on the road. When thus started, the team will

17.text: not stop until it reaches the next village, unless

18.text: the sledge should be overturned. Drivers not

19.text: over-confident tie the brake to the bow with

20.text: a strap, and avoid throwing it at the dogs.

21.text: Besides the brake, the Chukchee drivers

22.text: use a quirt with a short wooden handle and

23.text: a thick twisted lash (Fig. 29, a). The handle
23.note: mz/ocr keyed "(Fig, 20, a)." - comma instead of period after 'Fig' and '20' instead of '29'. Confirmed at 2x zoom: reads "(Fig. 29, a)."

24.text: has likewise a bunch of rings, and the driver

25.text: uses the quirt instead of the brake for intimi-

26.text: dating and punishing his animals. This quirt

27.text: is probably a modification of the former long-

28.text: lashed quirt of the Eskimo. A special whip

29.text: is used for punishing dogs (Fig. 29, b). It
29.note: mz/ocr keyed digit '6' for the italic figure-part letter; confirmed at 2x zoom it is italic 'b', matching Fig. 29's other part label 'a' on line 23.

30.text: has a longer handle and a lash with a very

31.text: slender end, also similar to the end of the

32.text: Eskimo quirt. Some of the dogs pull with

33.text: such energy that foam flows from their mouth,

34.text: their legs become strained, and they may die

36.text: at the start-off, with a heavy load, and before

37.text: the team is fairly under way. Other dogs are

38.text: lazy and shy, and will pull the trace just

39.text: enough to tighten it; they will even lean their

40.text: backs against the central strap for a while. Pups, when first harnessed, often

41.text: pull too obliquely, or lie down and are pulled along with the team. To prevent

42.text: this, their collar-straps are fastened with a thin line to the next loop-hole ahead.
